# One-page cheat sheet: I want to build X — which board should I buy?

# One-page cheat sheet: I want to build X — which board should I buy?

> Appendix to the Open Hardware Selection Handbook · GeekWaedon
> Original: https://www.zouic.com/articles/board-selection-cheatsheet/
> Price bands: ¥ = under ~CNY 30, ¥¥ = CNY 30-100, ¥¥¥ = above CNY 100

## Decision tree (locate in 30 seconds)
```text
First question: does the project need networking?
├─ Wi-Fi/Bluetooth ──→ Scenario 1
└─ Local control only ──→ Second question: battery-powered long-term?
    ├─ Yes, runtime-sensitive ──→ Scenario 3
    └─ Not sensitive / mains powered ──→ Scenarios 2 / 4 / 5
```

## Scenario cheatsheet (12 common cases)
| What you want to do | First choice | Alternative | Why | Pitfall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First IoT project (sensor reporting, remote switches) | ESP32-S3-DevKitC ¥¥ | ESP32-C3 ¥ | Most complete Espressif ecosystem, tutorials everywhere, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in | Buy the official DevKit; no-name boards have confusing pin labels |
| Learn embedded fundamentals (GPIO, interrupts, timers) | STM32F103C8T6 ¥ | Arduino UNO R4 ¥¥ | Register-level work teaches the fundamentals; most mature tutorial ecosystem | Needs a separate ST-Link programmer; watch out for clone chips |
| Battery-powered low power (sensor nodes, portables) | Raspberry Pi Pico ¥ | ESP32-C3 ¥ | RP2040 power control is simple and direct; dual cores are plenty | Pico has no Wi-Fi — choose Pico W (¥¥) if you need connectivity |
| Fast validation with the Arduino ecosystem | Arduino UNO R4 Minima ¥¥ | Nano ESP32 ¥¥ | Unbeatable library ecosystem; everything connects | UNO R4 switched to a Renesas chip; check library support before ordering |
| Edge AI inference (faces, object detection) | Sipeed Maixduino ¥¥ | — | The K210 has a built-in NPU, so inference does not depend on the cloud | Compute is limited — good for learning and lightweight deployment |
| Motor control / PID (balance bots, gimbals) | STM32F103C8T6 ¥ | STM32F407 ¥¥ | Rich timers, good real-time behaviour, plenty of FOC tutorials | Get open-loop control working before closing the loop |
| Industrial / CAN bus (automotive, data acquisition) | STM32F407ZGT6 ¥¥ | — | Native CAN controller | A CAN transceiver (e.g. TJA1050) still has to be added |
| Learn RISC-V (instruction set, architecture) | CH32V307 ¥ | GD32VF103 ¥ | Cheap and domestic; enough to learn the architecture properly | For a Linux-class RISC-V experience, see the next row |
| RISC-V + Linux (run a real OS) | VisionFive 2 ¥¥¥ | HiFive Unmatched ¥¥¥ | Runs a full Linux distribution, close to PC-style development | Not cheap — only for people who clearly need RISC-V Linux |
| Voice interaction (offline voice control) | ESP32-S3-DevKitC ¥¥ | — | Espressif's ESP-SR solution works out of the box | Offline vocabularies are limited; complex intent needs the cloud |
| Try a new protocol (NearLink) | NearLink DevKit Pro ¥¥ | Sensor Node ¥¥ | NearLink is early — joining now is a content opportunity | Few resources; suitable for experienced makers, not beginners |
| LoRa long-range communication (hundreds of metres to km) | ESP32-S3 + LoRa module ¥¥ | — | Add an SX1276 module to a Scenario 1 board — no need to change boards | Check local ISM band rules (470 MHz in China) |

## Three questions before ordering
1. Are there enough tutorials in your language? (Fewer than 10 decent ones means beginners should stay away.)
2. Do you need a separate programmer? (STM32 does; ESP32/Pico do not.)
3. Is the chip powerful enough for your project? (Work out compute needs first for camera or face-recognition work.)

## Reverse checklist (what you learn only after buying)
- Buy STM32 and you discover the programmer, jumper wires and breadboard are all extra — entry cost doubles.
- Buy a RISC-V Linux board and you discover ESP32 would have done the job, at a tenth of the price.
- Buy Pico and you discover networking needs an add-on module — you should have bought Pico W.
- Buy a no-name ESP32 and you discover the USB-serial chip is cut-rate and Windows drivers will not install.

## How this cheatsheet relates to the handbook
This page is the condensed version of the Open Hardware Selection Handbook. The full handbook covers pitfalls per board, eight complete project walkthroughs, toolchain checklists and how to identify genuine parts.
Chapter 1 is free to read: "The Right Order of Selection". Join the GeekWaedon Knowledge Planet for handbook updates and hands-on notes.

# The right order for board selection: scenario, constraints, then the board

# The right order for board selection: scenario, constraints, then the board

> "Open Hardware Selection Handbook" · Geek Weidong @GeekWaedon
> Original: https://www.zouic.com/articles/handbook-ch1/

## 1.1 A familiar script

You want to build something — say a temperature and humidity meter you can check remotely. You open a shopping site, search for "development board", sort by sales and find a board with impressive specs: a few hundred MHz, dozens of GPIOs, and "free tutorials included". The price is reasonable. You order.

Three days later the board arrives. Then you discover the tutorials are five years old, the bundled IDE will not install, and searching the error message returns three ancient posts on an English forum. A week later, the board goes in a drawer.

## 1.2 Wrong order vs right order

The wrong order (the instinct of 90% of beginners): specs → price → order → then figure out what to build.

The right order: scenario → constraints → board.

Why does the order matter so much? Because a development board is not a fast-moving consumer good — it is an entry point into an ecosystem. You are not just buying a PCB; you are buying the tutorials, libraries, community and documented pitfalls behind it. The clock speed on a spec sheet does not determine project success — the ecosystem does.

## 1.3 Step one: describe the scenario

"I want to build a smart device" is not a scenario, it is a wish. A proper scenario description answers four questions:

| Question | Example (remote temperature/humidity meter) |
| --- | --- |
| What are you building? | Collect temperature and humidity and report to a page you can view on your phone |
| Who is it for? | Myself, at home |
| Where will it go? | Living room with a power outlet — but I also want to try the balcony |
| How long will it run? | Always on, ideally unattended for months |

Fill in this template and you have already eliminated more than half of the candidate boards.

## 1.4 Step two: three typical constraints

Constraints filter the candidate set from "dozens of boards" down to "two or three". In order of importance:

**Networking.** No connectivity (local control, offline operation) → every MCU board remains a candidate Wi-Fi/Bluetooth → narrows to boards with built-in wireless such as the Espressif ESP32 family, Pico W and Arduino Nano ESP32 Long-range low power (hundreds of metres or more) → LoRa solutions, usually "main board + LoRa module" New protocol (NearLink) → the NearLink series, but accept that the ecosystem is still young

Many selection mistakes come from applying this filter last: you buy a board without wireless, discover halfway through that you need connectivity, and have to start over with an add-on module.

**Real-time requirements.** Ask yourself: if the system responds 0.1 seconds late, could that cause an accident? Yes (motor control, closed-loop PID, balance bots) → you need hard real-time; choose a traditional MCU such as STM32 and stay away from any board running Linux No (temperature/humidity reporting, human-machine interaction, data logging) → far more options, including Linux boards

A one-line test: any delay the human eye tolerates is fine for an MCU; any delay a motor cannot tolerate is unacceptable for Linux.

**Ecosystem maturity.** This is the highest-weight factor for beginners and can be relaxed for experienced makers. Check three things: Are there plenty of tutorials in your language? (Search the board model — if you find fewer than 10 decent tutorials, beginners should stay away.) Is there an existing library for every peripheral you plan to use? (OLED, servo, sensors — check each one.) Can you find answers to error messages? (Search the board model plus a common error keyword and see what comes back.)

This is why beginners are advised to start with ESP32 or STM32 — not because they are the most powerful, but because every step where you get stuck, someone has been stuck before and written down the answer.

Secondary constraints (budget, power consumption) come after these three. The reason is simple: the difference between ¥30 and ¥60 matters far less than whether you can finish the project at all.

## 1.5 A complete walkthrough

Back to the remote temperature/humidity meter from the opening. Here is the full reasoning:

Scenario: home use, living room/balcony, always on → Networking: Wi-Fi required, so all boards without wireless are out → Real-time: people read the numbers, half a second is fine → Ecosystem: first project, needs tutorials, Espressif wins → Secondary: budget-sensitive picks ESP32-C3, adding a screen picks ESP32-S3 → Conclusion: ESP32-S3-DevKitC or ESP32-C3-DevKitM.

The whole walkthrough takes less than two minutes, but every step has a reason. It does not guarantee the most powerful board — it guarantees a board you can finish the project with.

## 1.6 Three thinking traps

**Spec worship.**  "This one runs at 240 MHz and that one only 133 MHz, so buy the faster one." — The compute your temperature meter needs was available on chips twenty years ago. Excess specs will not make you succeed; a barren ecosystem will definitely make you fail.

**Architecture romance.**  "RISC-V is the future, I want to learn it in one go." — There is nothing wrong with believing in the architecture, but starting your first project on a RISC-V Linux board means facing three unknowns at once: a new architecture, a new OS and a new project. Challenge one layer at a time.

**One-board-for-everything.**  "Buy a board that can do everything, then I am set for any future project." — There is no do-everything board. Boards with Wi-Fi are not great at hard real-time; boards running Linux are not power-efficient. Development boards are consumables, not heirlooms.

## 1.7 Chapter checklist

- Have I written the four-part scenario? (what / who / where / how long)
- Is the networking requirement clear?
- Have I judged the real-time requirement?
- Have I counted tutorials for the candidate boards?
- Does every peripheral I need have an existing library?
- Is budget considered last?
- Am I choosing for this project, not for every future project?

**Next chapter:** 2.1 Wi-Fi/IoT workhorses — ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3, ESP32-C6 and BL602 compared: same Wi-Fi, double the price, what does the extra money buy?

Companion cheatsheet: One-Page Cheatsheet: I Want to Build X — Which Board Should I Buy? The handbook is updated continuously; join the GeekWaedon Knowledge Planet for new chapters.

# Don’t Build a Harvesting Business: Four Paid-Knowledge Models and the Compounding Alternative

# Don’t Build a Harvesting Business: Four Paid-Knowledge Models and the Compounding Alternative

> How Shengcaiyoushu, Qunxiang, Shen Ge and Xingdong Jiaoyu actually make money — and what a solo content site can sustain
> GeekWaedon · 2026-10-24
> Original: https://www.zouic.com/articles/knowledge-business-models

## 1. Why I wrote this

This site normally covers development boards and open hardware. This essay exists because of a more practical question: how does a content site with no funding and no team survive its third year?

Over the past two years I have watched a lot of paid-knowledge businesses: some became listed companies, some grew into private-domain operations with tens of millions in annual revenue, and some disappeared into refund disputes. What they share is not “selling knowledge” but “packaging a sense of scarcity into a sellable status”.

This is not a moral verdict; it is a structural breakdown. Which revenue compounds, and which only survives on constant acquisition? The conclusion up front: for a solo-run site like ZouIC, the right model is not a high-ticket community. It is public assets, low-ticket standard products, transparent subscriptions and outcome-based services.

## 2. Scope and boundaries

Sources are public reporting, company disclosures and public product pages, retrieved in October 2026. Prices and member counts change with time and promotions; the figures here illustrate structure only and do not confirm any organisation’s current pricing.

Descriptions of specific people and organisations only restate public reporting or public product information. They are not legal findings and do not characterise an entire business. Criticising a model and accusing a person are two different things.

One sourcing rule applies throughout: <strong>any sample whose product structure, pricing or delivery cannot be confirmed from verifiable public material is left out</strong>. Better one fewer case study than filling the gap with guesses.

## 3. Four verifiable samples, two revenue structures

Start with the table. Prices differ by nearly two orders of magnitude, yet there are only two revenue structures: selling status (membership, circles, private boards) or selling delivery (courses, managed services, consulting).

| Sample | Product structure | Public price band | Main revenue | Delivery focus | Public controversy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shengcaiyoushu | Annual membership UGC community | Tiered pricing; the public Knowledge Planet page shows CNY 3,365 per year in 2026 (lower during promotions) | Membership and renewals | Member-generated content, events, introductions | Value depends heavily on member initiative; anxiety marketing; content homogenisation |
| Qunxiang | Founder IP + private domain + high-ticket community | Basic membership around CNY 1,999; private board publicly quoted around CNY 49,800 | Membership, private board, events, matchmaking | Circle, information, offline setting | “Gathers people but does not land deals”; pressure selling in the room; light delivery |
| Shen Ge | IP matrix + tiered courses + private board + full-service packages | Courses CNY 2,980-9,980; private board CNY 80,000; full-service package CNY 2m per year | Courses, private board, managed accounts and packages | Methods, coaching, done-for-you accounts | Questionable reproducibility of case studies; public complaints of spend not matching results; accounts previously penalised for violations |
| Xingdong Jiaoyu | Listed management-training company | Compact EMBA publicly CNY 39,800 per person; Principal EMBA publicly CNY 498,000 per person (per public reporting and company materials) | Course orders, large clients, consulting | Standardised courses, tools, consulting | Sales-driven, high selling costs; “network success” criticism; prepaid model |

Selling status has high margins and scales fast, but burns trust just as fast. Selling delivery is heavier and slower, yet accumulates work and repeat purchases.

Xingdong Jiaoyu is a rare “both” case: standardised courses turn delivery into a repeatable product, while a sales force sells the sense of status. Because it is listed, its financials expose the real cost structure of this business — high gross margin sitting on top of even higher selling expenses.

## 4. Six observable traits of a harvesting offer

“Harvesting” is an emotional word, not an analytical tool. It is more useful to break it into six structural traits you can observe and self-check. Three or more is a warning; five or more usually means revenue comes from an ever-growing stream of new buyers rather than from delivery.

- [ ] Cash first, delivery later: the money is collected before delivery, and delivery has no acceptance criteria.
- [ ] Outcome promises replace process promises: “follow this and earn X a month” or “guaranteed account growth”, with no defined remedy for failure.
- [ ] Only the numerator is published: successful students are shown, while total enrolment, refund rate and average outcome are hidden.
- [ ] Decision-pressure design: deadlines, price increases, limited seats and countdowns push you to pay with incomplete information.
- [ ] Users become channels: resale commissions, referral unlocks and growth that depends on students recruiting students.
- [ ] Content does not persist: the core value exists only in livestreams and group chats, and vanishes when the group closes — impossible to review or enforce.

One more hidden trait: the refund barrier. Businesses that truly deliver can afford a plain “7-day, no questions asked” policy. Businesses that sell status tend to design a very long refund path.

## 5. Paying is not the sin: three dividing lines

Rejecting paid knowledge wholesale means missing genuinely valuable products. Three lines separate the healthy from the extractive:

- Verifiable delivery: you know before paying what you will get — quantity, format, timing and acceptance criteria are all explicit.
- Executable refunds: simple rules, a clear deadline, and no need to “convince support”.
- Growth without acquisition: renewals and repeat purchases sustain the base instead of starting from zero every month.

Meet all three and it is a transaction, however expensive. Meet none and it is an anxiety tax, however cheap.

## 6. What a compounding business actually is

“Dripping water wears through stone” does not mean “go slowly”. It means every drop lands on the same spot and leaves a mark. In business terms, that is four properties:

1. Asset accumulation: every investment leaves something reusable, searchable and transferable, rather than being consumed once.
2. Falling marginal cost: delivering to user 1,000 costs about the same as delivering to user one.
3. Trust compounding: the work is public and verifiable, so acquisition gets cheaper over time.
4. Cash flow without acquisition: revenue comes mainly from renewals, repeats and referrals rather than continuous ad spend.

Compare: a high-ticket private board satisfies half of the first property (it leaves relationships, not assets) and fails the second and fourth. A standardised course satisfies the second, but if a sales force drives it, the fourth rarely holds. What satisfies all four is usually “public content + tools or databases + standard products + outcome-priced services”.

## 7. What ZouIC already has

Listing existing assets matters more than debating which new project to start:

- A bilingual site of 140+ pages, fully static, with near-zero annual running cost.
- A maintained board database and project index, naturally suited to search and AI citation.
- Reusable structured content: selection methods, cheat sheets and handbook chapters.
- Website-building and GEO managed services, with a real case study — this site itself.
- WeCom service-provider status, which supports private-domain and customer-management work.
- Same-name accounts across WeChat, Zhihu and Bilibili for distribution and trust.

What these assets share: they do not require someone online in real time, and they can be found, cited and reused. That is the spot where the water lands.

## 8. A four-layer revenue structure

| Layer | Product | Price band | Delivery | Repeat source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L0 Public assets | Board database, project index, selection guides, articles | Free | Automatically served by the site | Search traffic and trust |
| L1 Standard products | Cheat sheets, handbook e-book, templates, checklists | CNY 9.9-99 | Automatic, no human involvement | Word of mouth and content |
| L2 Subscription | Knowledge Planet, column, update newsletter | Up to CNY 365/year | Fixed monthly posts + archive + Q&A SLA | Renewals |
| L3 Services | Website building, GEO managed service, WeCom solutions | From CNY 3,000 / from CNY 1,500 per month | Project-based, milestone acceptance | Case studies and referrals |

The four layers form a funnel, not a menu: L0 gets you found, L1 validates demand, L2 stabilises cash flow, L3 produces profit. None of them should close a sale through pressure tactics.

For a solo operator, L1 is the most underrated: a CNY 29 cheat sheet sold 1,000 times is CNY 29,000 with almost no added delivery cost, and it validates demand for L2 and L3. L2 is the most overrated: a community needs continuous presence, and quality inevitably drops as it scales.

## 9. A one-year sequence

1. Q1: thicken L0. Cover 20 high-frequency selection scenarios, attach downloadable structured data to each article, and set a fixed publishing calendar.
2. Q2: build L1. Turn cheat sheets, handbook chapters and website checklists into standalone digital products with one price list and one refund policy.
3. Q3: open L2. Promise only what can be delivered: four hands-on notes a month, a quarterly livestream, a searchable archive and a reply within 48 hours. Keep the price under CNY 365 and optimise for renewal, not scale.
4. Q4: scale L3. Acquire through public case studies and a portfolio, not sales events or countdown pressure. Write delivery into an SOP; take fewer projects rather than ones beyond capacity.

Add one layer per quarter. Opening all four at once usually means doing all four badly.

## 10. What not to do

This negative list matters more than the to-do list:

- Do not promise income, follower growth or account success — promise content and dates.
- Do not run headcount recruitment, resale commissions or per-head interest schemes.
- Do not use fake deadlines, fake scarcity or fake price increases.
- Do not sell “connections” or “the circle” as the main deliverable.
- Do not take coaching or full-service work beyond your delivery capacity.
- Do not create value that exists only inside a group chat and disappears when it closes.
- Do not use “everyone else is making money” as the main argument.

## 11. Ten questions before you publish

- [ ] Before paying, can the buyer know exactly what they will get?
- [ ] Can the deliverable be counted, searched and accepted?
- [ ] Can the refund rule be stated in one sentence?
- [ ] If 80% of buyers never act, is the product still worth the price?
- [ ] How much revenue comes from renewals and referrals?
- [ ] How many hours does one customer take, and does that hold at ten times the scale?
- [ ] Have anxiety, comparison or scarcity replaced real value?
- [ ] Do the case studies disclose sample size and failures alongside successes?
- [ ] What remains after the group closes or the updates stop?
- [ ] In three years, will this make acquisition easier or harder?

## 12. Conclusion

**Conclusion**

> For ZouIC, the right move is not “build a high-ticket community”. It is to turn the open-hardware information gap into public assets, validate demand with low-ticket standard products, stabilise cash flow with a transparent subscription, and earn profit from outcome-based services. The path is slow, but every drop lands on the same spot.

Harvesting models earn from information gaps and human nature. Information gaps disappear; human nature does not — so the model always has a market, and always needs new traffic. Compounding models earn from time and work: slow at first, lighter later. Choosing one is really choosing who you will be in three years.

## Disclaimer

This is a business-analysis essay, not investment, legal or purchasing advice. Prices, member counts and revenue figures come from public reporting or public product pages, may use different definitions or be out of date, and are cited without verification. Nothing here is an allegation against any person or organisation.
